claims.text: The ab initio Z-method can determine the melting temperature of high-melting refractory materials.
The ab initio Z-method can determine entropy of fusion.
The ab initio Z-method can determine enthalpy of fusion.
The ab initio Z-method can determine the volume change at melting.
The Z-method avoids the full thermodynamic integration required by the conventional ab initio free-energy approach.
The Z-method is computationally less expensive than full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The proposed implementation rapidly heats a simulation cell in a microcanonical constant-energy ensemble until spontaneous melting occurs.
Application of the method requires a superheated metastable crystalline state near the melting transition.
Melting proceeds through an evolving solid-liquid interface or a homogeneous transformation in a single cell.
Spontaneous melting is marked by a sharp change in internal energy.
Spontaneous melting is marked by a sharp change in volume.
Thermodynamic discontinuities observed during melting permit estimation of melting temperature, latent heat, fusion entropy, and volume change.
Fusion entropy can be computed from fusion enthalpy and melting temperature using ΔS_f = ΔH_f/T_m.
Z-method results will agree within acceptable deviations with results from full ab initio free-energy integration.
Systems with complex melting behavior or rugged energy landscapes may have larger uncertainties under the Z-method.
Estimated fusion enthalpy and entropy may be sensitive to simulation-cell size.
Estimated fusion enthalpy and entropy may be sensitive to the dynamics of the melting process.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies a constant-energy microcanonical trajectory, while the mechanism identifies spontaneous melting through a sharp change in internal energy. Total internal energy cannot undergo such a change within a single strictly constant-energy trajectory; the intended temperature drop or comparison across separately initialized energies is not stated.

A standard microcanonical simulation cell has fixed volume, yet the mechanism and outcome claim that a volume discontinuity will be obtained. No variable-volume ensemble, pressure condition, equation-of-state procedure, or set of simulations at different volumes is specified.
